en: Preface to the Commentary on the Heart Sūtra:
Now, empty space is fundamentally non-existent. Yet from it arises qi, and from qi arises form;
from form arises mind, from mind arises speech, and from speech arises the sūtra. Thus, since the mind exists as something existent, who would doubt that it is non-existent? Nevertheless...
The essence of the body of emptiness remains as it is; because it is sovereign, it is called "non-existent.

As for what is stated in the Sūtra—from "from the non-existence of the eye-sphere" up to "by means of non-apprehension"—these thirteen characters flow in continuous succession like linked pearls, impossible to obstruct.

Furthermore, how could there be anything else? Since the person is non-existent, phenomena naturally must be non-existent; therefore, it is said that "all phenomena have the characteristic of emptiness. The person...
When all phenomena are empty together, then the mind is fundamentally without mind, and even the sutras are without sutras.

Contemplating emptiness and entering meditative concentration, one realizes that "I" and "Heaven" are one; yet Heaven, conversely, cannot overcome its existence. It is precisely because Heaven cannot overcome its existence that it is Heaven;
whereas the Buddha cannot overcome his non-existence, and thus he differs from Heaven. A skillful student awakens to this identity with Heaven, and further awakens to...

To differ from Heaven means that existence is not merely existence, and non-existence is not merely non-existence; it is neither existence nor non-existence, yet neither is it the negation of existence and non-existence.
Thus, movement and stillness serve as mutual roots, whereby one may return to Confucianism and enter the Way.
Preface by the Layman Laiyun Zhu Wanli on the Mid-Autumn Day of the Ding-si Year of the Wanli Era.
Commentary on the Heart Sutra by the Layman Laiyun Zhu Wanli of Shanyin. Translated and annotated by Zhù Wànlǐ.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.
*Mahā* means "great. *Prajñā* means "wisdom. *Pāra* means "the other shore. *Mi* means "secret" (or "mystery"). *Ta* means "multitude.
*Hṛdaya* means "essence" (or "heart"). *Sūtra* means "path. It refers to taking the essence of the mind as the path for all practices. However, wisdom is not...
"Cleverness" refers to the functioning of the emotional consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness is subject to birth and death; awakening is without gain and without loss.
When active, one is not deceived by external objects; when still, one does not stagnate in the vast emptiness. This alone constitutes wisdom. Furthermore, what is meant by "the other shore"?
It is said that those who are deluded regarding birth and death remain "here," while those who transcend birth and death are "there. Originally, there is no [distinction].
The "limits" (yān) are distinguished according to the mind's own functioning. Furthermore, what is meant by "Guhyaka"?

It refers to the smelting [of all things] into a single flavor—the pure *tathatā* (true suchness) of the *gotra* (spiritual lineage)—harmonized and free from admixture. What is the *Hṛdaya-sūtra*? It states that stillness is the very substance of the mind;
outside of stillness there is no mind, and outside of the mind there is no path. This is the meaning of its name.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
A bodhisattva is none other than a Buddha. Why is it that the mind is without hindrance? It is because he looks back and illuminates within with such mastery;
this is so at all times. Here, his name is cited to honor him. "Practice" (*xing*) refers to cultivation. "Profound" (*shen*) means subtle. This is what is being said.
The Bodhisattva practices and reaches the subtle and wondrous state; this is the introductory statement of the author of this sutra.
At that time, Śāriputra, he perceived that the five aggregates are all empty, and thereby transcended all suffering and distress.

"Time" refers to the present. The "five aggregates" (pañca-skandha) are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Form is characterized by emptiness and resistance; sensation is the experiencing of objects;
perception is conceptualization; mental formations are movement; and consciousness is discrimination. They are called "aggregates" because they accumulate and store.

Due to the non-dissipation of habitual tendencies, one falsely identifies the physical body as the self, and thus wanders in saṃsāra for long eons. Only the consciousness of a Bodhisattva [is exempt from this].

To realize that the physical body is an illusion, one should constantly reflect inwardly. Thus illuminating the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), they are seen to be utterly pure and clearly discerned.
One perceives the fundamental nature of objects; encountering things, one does not cling to them. One is not stained by the two realms of sound and form, and the mind does not grasp at them.

One does not dwell on the past nor calculate the future. Not turned by external objects and not lingering after chasing after circumstances, one makes no distinctions among things, treating them all with uniformity.
Equanimity is spontaneous. The four great elements are not the self; the six sense faculties are collectively void.
Thus one transcends birth and death, escapes the cycle of saṃsāra, and becomes a perfected immortal. *Śaya* means "house"; *Śāriputra* means "the original essence within the house.

This signifies that while all manifold delusions are empty, the void-spiritual awareness does not perish. Song Jingliao stated that *dukkha* (suffering) refers to various afflictions. Cold... [text truncated]
Furthermore, not obtaining clothing is suffering; being hungry and not obtaining food is suffering; being weary and not obtaining rest is suffering;
being ill and not obtaining recuperation is suffering, and so forth. It is feared that the Bodhisattva likewise has no such sufferings as these.
"Transcending all speech. To transcend that [the external] while guarding this [the internal] is *śarīra*. Śāriputra gathered these as beads;
therefore, they are called "sons" (*śarī*). When contemplating the Buddha and the patriarchs, one should also carry them in mind.

According to Zongle’s commentary, Śāri was a disciple of the Buddha; because he was inquiring on behalf of the assembly, [the Buddha] called out to him and addressed him, thus treating Śāri as a person.
Furthermore, according to the second honored Arhat, there is a lapis lazuli bottle before him containing several dozen śarīras;
thus, he is not a human being either. In my humble opinion, neither the preceding nor the following passages mention a disciple.

Such phrasing stands out as a single passage; its literary logic appears incoherent. Furthermore, since the subsequent text again addresses the disciple by name, it would be even more meaningless [to treat this as a separate unit].

However, the *Bisheng* records that when the various bodhisattvas in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* discussed the Dharma-gate of non-duality, Śāriputra remained silent, and the heavenly maiden did not approve of this; this was because she regarded Śāriputra as a disciple. Let us examine this more closely.
Form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, Śāriputra.

As for the five aggregates, they are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Since form is the foremost among the five aggregates, the character "form" (rūpa) encompasses them all.
One attains the four aggregates. Since the five aggregates are empty, form is not different from emptiness; since the five aggregates are empty, emptiness is not different from form.
Yet it is not merely that they are not different; form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.
Originally there are no two characteristics; they are in reality one and the same. For although the aggregate of form is empty, there is no place where form is absent. This is because...

As for true form (*rūpa*), the [remaining] four aggregates (*skandha*) can be understood by extension. The eye is form, yet it cannot see; only the wondrous nature (*prajñā*) can see—this seeing is true seeing.
If the locus of seeing is true seeing, then the four lower aggregates can likewise be understood. Thus, the real is not false, and the false is the real.
True form is moreover formless. How does form differ from emptiness (*śūnyatā*)? That which is formless is true form; how does emptiness differ [from it]?
Form is distinct; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise as form is—all take emptiness as their form.

This states that the five aggregates are fundamentally empty, and it is through this that all suffering and affliction are transcended. Thus, the phrase "the mark of the emptiness of all phenomena" is established.
Zongle said: "Sentient beings are deluded regarding true emptiness and thus undergo illusory form, just as water turns into ice.
Bodhisattvas, by practicing *prajñā*, recognize true emptiness, which is like melting ice back into water. Yet, as for form and emptiness, their essence is no different;
therefore it is said that 'form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form,' just as ice [is not different from water]."

Water is not different from ice, and ice is not different from water. Yet, fearing that sentient beings of dull faculties might fail to understand and still persist in the two views of form and emptiness, it is said:
"Form is identical to emptiness; emptiness is identical to form. This is like saying water is identical to water, and water is identical to ice.
Such a metaphor is indeed apt. Nevertheless, it is clearly stated: sentient beings are deluded regarding the Truth, and furthermore, they possess dull faculties.
That sentient beings do not understand this can be known as not being the self-cultivation of a bodhisattva.
These dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness: they are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Therefore, within emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Although the five aggregates are illusory thoughts, the *dharmakāya* is precisely these five aggregates; therefore, they are called "all phenomena" (*dharmas*). Form is itself emptiness.
One can see that all phenomena possess the characteristic of emptiness, and characteristics are themselves form. Since characteristics are empty, both arising and ceasing are empty.
Arising is itself ceasing; what could increase, and what could decrease? Both defilement and purity are empty.
Defilement is itself purity. What is defiled, and what is pure? Both increase and decrease are empty. Increase is itself decrease.
What is increased, and what is decreased? Birth, cessation, defilement, purity, increase, and decrease—all are but the marks of form within emptiness.
Without these six characteristics, what form could there be? If there is no form, how can there be sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
As for consciousness: at this point, one has only mastered the single phrase, "the five aggregates are all empty.
(Xianshou said: "Neither arising nor ceasing" refers to the stage before the Way—the ordinary person in the mundane state who dies here and is born there, transmigrating through long kalpas;
this is the stage of arising and ceasing. True emptiness transcends this, and therefore it is called neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor...)

"Purity" refers to the stages of the bodhisattva on the path; that is, those bodhisattvas whose defilements and obscurations are not yet exhausted, yet who have already cultivated pure conduct—this is called the stage of "defiled purity.
Since true emptiness is free from these, it is said to be "neither defiled nor pure. As for "neither increasing nor decreasing":

There is the stage of the fruition of Buddhahood after the Path has been attained. As for the delusions and hindrances of birth and death, they were not yet exhausted in the past but are now exhausted; this is "diminution.

As for the myriad virtues produced through cultivation, they were not yet perfected in the past but are now perfected; this is "augmentation. True Emptiness is free from these two states; therefore, it is said to be "neither increasing nor decreasing."

In my humble opinion, regarding the six characters "arising and ceasing," "defilement and purity," and "increase and decrease," one may distinguish between arising and ceasing, and defilement and purity, such that even the fruit of Buddhahood can be so categorized.
However, since [the Buddha-nature] proceeds from the empty characteristic of all phenomena, as discussed above, the myriad virtues are already perfected; it is thus spontaneous and natural.

Furthermore, how could there be three positions? For the "three" are not identical to the "three absences. An "absence" (*wu*) is a state of total non-existence; a "not" (*bu*) is an absence that leaves a trace.
In the empty and void world, what is there to be "not" or "absent"? From where, then, could boundaries and distinctions be demarcated?
This was spoken again for those of dull faculties; it should not be followed.
No eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or mental phenomenon; no眼界 (eye-element) up to and including no consciousness-element.

The aggregates (*skandha*) are connected with the sense-faculties (*indriya*). The aggregates are the soil for the seeds of the faculties; the faculties are the roots of the flowers and trees. The five aggregates...

Because they are empty, the six sense organs are also empty. Just as the eye, though it sees, does not cling to forms—when it does not cling to forms, it is no different from having no eyes at all—the same applies to the five lower organs.
When the six sense organs are pure, one is naturally untainted by the six sense objects.
Since one is untainted by the six sense objects, what forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena could there be? All six sense objects arise from the sense organs.

Arising from above, one simply reflects back upon the sense-faculties themselves. When the six faculties cease, the six objects also cease; even the two faculties of the eye and the mind cease without exception.
To rely on the eye is the demonic army that obstructs the Way; to become attached to objects is to lose one's way through self-delusion.
When the realm of the eye is pure, the realm of the mind is at peace, and the eighteen realms naturally become tranquil. This is also the essential method for severing the six sense-faculties.
The Secret Instruction. Therefore it is said: "When the eyes observe and the mind moves, one becomes attached to objects and loses sight of the Truth. (Zongle says:
Within the marks of true emptiness, there are likewise no six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) and no six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). This is the emptiness of the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).

Since the twelve bases do not exist, the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*) also do not exist. As for the eighteen realms, they consist of the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the [six consciousnesses]...)
"Consciousness" is it. Regarding the phrase "and so forth," this refers to the beginning and the end, with the "elements" (dhātus) included therein.

As for the aforementioned five aggregates (skandhas), twelve bases (āyatanas), and eighteen elements, they do not transcend the two dharmas of form and mind. For those whose delusion regarding the mind is predominant, they are taught as the five aggregates;

for those whose delusion regarding form is predominant, they are taught as the twelve bases; and for those who are deluded regarding both form and mind, they are taught as the ten... [eighteen elements].
The eight elements. Regarding the three categories above, a person who practices and studies according to their faculties need only cultivate one category to be able to realize and enter [the truth].
(Song Jingliao said: "The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are called the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). They are like the roots of plants and trees.")

It is also called the six entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*). "Roots" (*indriya*) refers to what is internal; "entrances" (*āyatana*) refers to what is external. Seeing with the eyes constitutes the dust of form (*rūpa-rajas*);

hearing with the ears constitutes the dust of sound (*śabda-rajas*); smelling with the nose constitutes the dust of fragrance (*gandha-rajas*); tasting with the tongue constitutes the dust of flavor (*rasa-rajas*); touching with the body constitutes the dust of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya-rajas*);

and mental attachment constitutes the dust of phenomena (*dharma-rajas*). These are called the six dusts (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). They are so named because they obstruct and veil one, like particles of sand and dust.
Furthermore, the union of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) constitutes the twelve bases (*āyatana*). A "base" is a locus. From seeing arises visual consciousness;
from hearing, auditory consciousness; from smelling, olfactory consciousness; from tasting, gustatory consciousness; from touching, tactile consciousness;

and from conceptualization, mental consciousness. These are called the six consciousnesses. The union of these three [faculties, objects, and consciousnesses] constitutes the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). An "element" is a limit.
It is because sentient beings are mired in birth and death due to these three factors mutually entangling and drawing one another in, preventing them from escaping.
Within true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), none of these ever existed from the beginning.

I, the fool, examine the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses; these are called the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*). Those who can awaken to them are themselves eighteen venerable Arhats;
those who cannot awaken to them are themselves the eighteen layers of hell. How does one awaken to them? By realizing that they are non-existent from the very beginning.
How does one become deluded? By perceiving existence and clinging to existence. For one who clings to them, it lasts for a lifetime.
There is no abandoning of the other shore for Avīci; it is not merely eighteen layers.
There is neither ignorance nor the exhaustion of ignorance, and so on, up to neither old age and death nor the exhaustion of old age and death.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the absence of light; all manner of afflictions arise from it. Because of ignorance, there are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*);

because of volitional formations, there is consciousness (*vijñāna*); because of consciousness, there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); because of name-and-form, there are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); because of the six sense bases, there is contact (*sparśa*);

because of contact, there is sensation (*vedanā*); because of sensation, there is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); because of craving, there is grasping (*upādāna*); because of grasping, there is becoming (*bhava*).
Because of existence there is birth; because of birth there is old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction—all of which originate from ignorance as their beginning.
If one can personally perceive and subdue ignorance, the three poisons will naturally be extinguished and the evil roots eradicated.

Yet this very ignorance is the true nature, which is itself the Buddha-nature. When this true nature undergoes a single transformation, one is a Buddha—just as stinginess and greed are transformed [into generosity and virtue].
They rejoice, foolishly clinging to this as a state of perfect integration and liberation. Yet, with such a turn, how could ignorance ever be exhausted?
Because they turn without reaching the point of exhaustion, it is utterly non-existent.

People possess ignorance (*avidyā*), which is nothing other than the fear of birth and death. Once ignorance is absent, what further cause for anxiety remains regarding birth, old age, sickness, and death?
Since there is no longer aging and death, this state remains thus throughout eternal kalpas; how could it ever come to an end? That which has an end is the illusory form-body (*rūpakāya*);
that which has no end is the dharma-characteristic of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The illusory body is transformed into the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
How could one possibly attain them all? At the point of exhaustion, there is emptiness, where neither old age nor death exists; at the point of exhaustion, there is only the perception of emptiness.
In sum, it is simply this single phrase: within emptiness, there is no form. For existence is indeed non-existence, and non-existence is likewise non-existence.

(Zongle said: "This is the emptiness of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). They are also called the twelve factors (*dvādaśāṅga*). First is ignorance (*avidyā*), also named affliction (*kleśa*).
Second is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), meaning the performance of various karmic actions. These two factors are the causes produced in the past.
Third is consciousness (*vijñāna*), meaning the arising of deluded thoughts and the initial entry into the mother’s womb. Fourth is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). From [the moment of] entry..."*

Following the stage of the embryo (*kalala*), there arises the formation of the sense faculties and their physical forms. Fifth is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*): within the womb, the six faculties are completed. Sixth is contact (*sparśa*):

after the formation of the embryo, the six faculties encounter the six objects. Seventh is sensation (*vedanā*): this refers to the experiencing of worldly things, such as the pleasant and the unpleasant.
These five links constitute the fruits experienced in the present life. Eighth is craving (*tṛṣṇā*): this refers to greedy attachment.
The five objects of desire and so forth. Ninth is grasping (*upādāna*): this refers to the arising of a mind of attachment toward various objects. Tenth is existence (*bhava*):
this refers to creating the causes for outflow (*āsrava*) that can summon future results. These three links constitute the causes produced in the present. Eleventh is birth (*jāti*):
this refers to receiving a body composed of the five aggregates (*skandha*) in the future. Twelfth is old age (*jarā*).
"Death" refers to the future body; having grown old, one dies. These two links are the fruits to be experienced in a future life.
These twelve links of dependent origination encompass the causes and effects of the three periods of time, revolving in succession like a wheel without ceasing.
That all sentient beings are deluded and do not understand this is truly to be pitied. This is originally for those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
The object of contemplation is that all Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas thoroughly perceive this realm as having no real nature; therefore, it is said to be "non-existent.
Examining this section, it is precisely a discourse on saṃsāra. Yet, though it appears to exist, it is in reality non-existent.

As for the existence or non-existence of saṃsāra, how could it be divided according to the two faculties of the sharp and the dull? If it exists, it exists for both; if it does not exist, it does not exist for both. Great...
Because Zongle was of a dull faculty, his words were thus fragmented and disjointed.
There is no suffering, no karma, no cessation, and no path; there is no wisdom, nor is there anything to be attained, because there is nothing to be attained.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva relies upon the Prajñāpāramitā.
Once one forgets their physical form, birth and death are immediately severed and can never again be exhausted. What then remains of suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path?
Suffering exists in contrast to pleasure; yet in the bliss of emptiness, that bliss is sovereign. From where, then, could suffering arise?
Is it not said that one transcends all suffering and calamity? Extinction (*nirodha*) is simply exhaustion. Since there is no exhaustion, how could there be extinction or non-extinction?
Thus, the Way is eternally sovereign. Is it not said that it cannot be worn away throughout ten thousand kalpas?

If this is so, then wisdom has no function to employ, and even "attainment" is devoid of anything attained. The character for "attainment" does not carry the character for "wisdom"; it is because of attainment...
This is precisely the attainment of wisdom. Once the state of attainment is reached, what further need is there for wisdom?
Indeed, wisdom is indispensable at certain times and unnecessary at others. When advancing on the Path, it must be present; once the Path is attained, it must be absent.
This is what is meant by "truly having nothing attained. It is called "attaining the Path" only for the sake of transforming sentient beings. Since there is nothing attained, [it is] the One Body.
It is empty and void. By nature, both persons and phenomena are empty. Because one has attained the power of great wisdom, one ascends to the other shore;
yet that Great Void is such that nothing can equal it. For those who follow the view of persons, there is "attainment"; for those who follow the view of self, there is "non-attainment.
Non-attainment is itself attainment—it is simply attaining that which is non-existent. This is precisely the absence of suffering and its accumulation (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*).
The Stage of Cessation and the Path (Zhongle says:
There is no suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path; this is the contemplation of the purity of the Four Noble Truths. Suffering refers to the fruit of suffering within birth and death.)
The "accumulation" (samudaya) is the cause of afflictions, karma, and suffering; these three are the phenomena of the mundane world.

"Cessation" (nirodha) is the blissful fruit of nirvana, and the "path" (mārga) is the blissful cause consisting of the factors of enlightenment; these two are the phenomena of the supramundane world. These Four Noble Truths are thus taught.
It is intended to cause sentient beings to know suffering and sever its accumulation, to aspire toward cessation and cultivate the path, thereby leaving suffering behind and attaining happiness.

This is originally the realm contemplated by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle; however, when Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas illuminate and comprehend this realm, they realize that its very substance is empty and quiescent.
Therefore, it is said to be "non-existent."
The fool says that it begins from "no-form in emptiness," followed by ten consecutive instances of the character for "non-existence" (wu). This may be called the ultimate limit of non-existence;
reaching this point, one ought not to speak again of the two terms "worldly cause and effect. For there would be neither suffering nor cessation.
Wisdom has already been exhausted. If there is something attained, yet one does not know that there is no attainment, then wisdom is merely for the sake of attainment.

Since there is nothing to be attained, what further use is there for wisdom? This is what is meant by "within emptiness there is no form. When the fundamental principle and its exposition do not coincide, it is not so.
(Song Jingliao said: "Not only are all the aforementioned phenomena non-existent within emptiness, but even that wisdom which knows emptiness cannot be apprehended.
Not only can the wisdom that knows emptiness not be apprehended, but even this principle of emptiness that is known cannot be attained.

This is because the nature of the single truth does not depend on cultivation or realization, for it is utterly devoid of even a single dharma. I, the fool, say: "This is precisely what constitutes a person.")
(These words speak of the emptiness inherent in all phenomena).
When the mind is without hindrance, because it is without hindrance, there is no fear; far removed from perverted views and delusions, one attains ultimate Nirvana.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
To have continuous thoughts and perceptions is called "entanglement" (saṅga); if a mirror does not face a face, it is called "obstruction" (āvaraṇa).

Since one has already ascended to the other shore and harmonized with the spiritual lineage (gotra), all conditions are liberated and dispersed. What, then, is entanglement? What is obstruction? What is fear? What is inversion? What are dreams and delusions?
There is neither birth nor death; quiescent extinction is bliss. Together with the Buddhas of the three periods of time, all are entirely non-existent. As for the "three periods":
these are the one thousand adorned Buddhas of the past, the one thousand star-constellation Buddhas of the future, and the one thousand Buddhas of the Worthy Eon in the present.
They also exist within the human body. If the mind is without that [conceptual] mind, this is the transcendence of the past.

The Buddha who has departed is quiescent and unmoving; this is the future Buddha. The Samādhi of Responsive Manifestation, which transforms according to the capacities of beings, is the present Buddha.
Each and every Buddha exists within one's own body; like space, they are without any difference in appearance.
It is not characterized by self, nor characterized by other; it is neither signless, nor is it the grasping of signs. It is not this shore, not the other shore, and not the middle current.
To contemplate its quiescent extinction, which is eternally non-ceasing—this alone is the ultimate, this alone is ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
By relying on wisdom, one ascends to the other shore; through the harmonization of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), one is thus able to fulfill and achieve perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"A-nou-duo-lo" (Anuttara) means "Unsurpassed"; "San-miao" (Samyak) means "Correct"; "San-pu-ti" (Sambodhi) means "True Awakening.
In the Eastern Land [China], it is translated as "Unsurpassed, Correct, and True," or alternatively, "Attaining Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.

It refers to a vast and sudden awakening, wherein one personally perceives the Unsurpassed, Correct, and True, knowing for oneself that one shall become an Immortal-Buddha and directly transcend to the fruit of sainthood. This is the ultimate of spiritual practice; observe for yourself—
For the Bodhisattva, it is simply a matter of contemplating this alone.
Therefore, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, and an unequaled mantra;
it is able to eliminate all suffering, being true and not false.
By relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and true awakening. This single phrase of mantra is a great divine mantra;
"divine" refers to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). It is a great illuminating mantra; "illuminating" refers to radiance. It is the unsurpassed mantra.
Among all dharmas, this is the foremost. It is the peerless mantra; it is the ultimate pinnacle of the sublime. Every person possesses this mantra.
The illumination of the mind and the realization of nature both emerge from this. Once one has attained the realization of nature, what suffering or calamity could there be?
This is the discourse of the true Dharma; it is not empty or flowery speech. (Zongle says:
The four kinds of mantras refer to the function of Prajñā. Because it can destroy demonic obstacles, it is called the Great Divine Mantra.

Because it can extinguish the darkness of ignorance, it is called the Great Illuminating Mantra. Because it can reveal the ultimate principle, it is called the Unsurpassed Mantra. It is the most wondrous awakening.)
The fruit is peerless; it is called the "Spell of the Peerless. These words are likewise so:

they can destroy demonic obstacles, and by destroying the darkness of ignorance, they reveal the ultimate principle. To reveal the ultimate principle is itself the fruit of supreme, wondrous awakening.
If one speaks directly from this point downward, one’s self-awakening will be secure and stable; yet, regarding the finality of the principle, one must never fail to practice.
Since the tenets and the explanations are likewise non-existent, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā mantra is spoken; the mantra is as follows:
*gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*.
The efficacy of the Prajñā dhāraṇī is the greatest. This single phrase alone should not be treated lightly; it must be brought forth.
The four-line verse that follows provides protection for those who uphold the sūtra. *Prajñe* refers to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Another *prajñe* refers to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). When both persons and phenomena are empty, the two types of emptiness are completely forgotten. *Pāraprajñe* refers to the emptiness of non-existence.
That which is empty, the other shore is also empty. *Pārasaṃgate* means the pure realm of all Buddhas, that which is collectively experienced by the thousands of sages and worthies.

*Bodhi svāhā* means that when one first gives rise to the bodhicitta, without further conceptualization, one suddenly awakens to the Way, realizes the emptiness of the fundamental nature, and thereby attains bodhi.

There is no profound secret meaning [here].孤山 (Gushan) said: "Even if a master of the scriptures can skillfully explain the meanings and purports, causing heavenly flowers to fall in profusion, it only serves to block the path to the Gate of Emptiness.
Therefore, he concludes with a divine spell (*dhāraṇī*). Thus, although there may be those who possess skillful understanding, there is none...
"It can accommodate its beak. I, the fool, believe that the words "the Gate of Emptiness is blocked" contain the most profound reason.
The gate is fundamentally empty, yet when it is blocked by earth, does this not constitute an obstruction? This is most wondrous.
Commentary on the Heart Sutra (End)
